opening: Our engineers currently SSH into machines to read logs, which doesn't scale anymore. Let's design a central pipeline that collects logs from all our servers and makes them searchable. Where would you start?

clarifications.answer: About 5,000 hosts across 3 regions, most running containers on Kubernetes.
Around 500,000 log lines a second in total, about 400 bytes each on average.
During incidents volume can jump to about 5 times normal for an hour or more.
Engineers want to search and filter the last 7 days, and see a line within 30 seconds of it being written.
Everything is kept for 1 year for audits. Older than 7 days is rarely queried and can be slow to search.
Security and audit logs must never be dropped. Debug logs may be sampled when needed.
Most services log JSON, but some legacy apps write plain text lines.
Logs sometimes accidentally contain tokens, emails or card numbers; those must not be stored.

clarificationPolicy: Answer as the observability team lead. Keep it a high-volume log ingestion and search problem; decide unlisted details so buffering, tiering and burst behaviour stay central.

agenda.goal: Establish volume, burst behaviour, search freshness, retention and which logs are critical.
agenda.opener: What do you need to know about the logs and how engineers use them?

evidence.strong: Asks about host count, lines per second and line size, burst behaviour during incidents, search freshness and range, retention and audits, which classes can't be lost, formats and sensitive data; estimates daily volume.
evidence.adequate: Gets volume and retention but not bursts or which logs are critical.
evidence.weak: Starts with a tool name without asking about volume or retention.

misconceptions.challenge: When does log volume peak, and is that when engineers most need search?

probes: How much data a day does that add up to?
hints: Ask whether some logs are legally required.
agenda.moveOnSummary: Hundreds of thousands of lines a second with incident bursts, seven-day fast search, a year of cheap retention, and security logs that must never drop.

agenda.goal: Collect logs from every host reliably into a durable buffer.
agenda.opener: How do logs get off each host and into the pipeline?

evidence.strong: A lightweight agent on each host (Fluent Bit or Vector, as a DaemonSet on Kubernetes) tails files and container output, batches, compresses and buffers to disk, and ships to regional collectors that write to Kafka topics per log class.
evidence.adequate: Uses agents but sends directly to the search cluster, or has no buffering on the host.
evidence.weak: Has applications write logs straight to a database or the search cluster over the network.

misconceptions.pattern: Thinks agents can send straight to the search cluster.
misconceptions.challenge: The search cluster slows down during an incident. Where do logs go while it can't keep up?

probes: What does the agent do if the network to the collectors is down?
Why put a log broker in the middle?
hints: The host should be able to hold logs for a while.
Decouple producers from the indexing tier.
agenda.moveOnSummary: Per-host agents with disk buffers and batching ship to collectors that write to Kafka topics per log class.

agenda.goal: Store recent logs for fast search and older logs cheaply.
agenda.opener: Where do logs live so engineers search recent ones quickly but a year of history stays affordable?

evidence.strong: A hot search tier (OpenSearch, Elasticsearch, Loki or ClickHouse) holds recent logs in time-based indices with lifecycle rollover; an archive of compressed files in object storage, partitioned by date and service, holds a year and is queried with Athena or Trino or rehydrated on demand.
evidence.adequate: Has two tiers but no lifecycle policy or way to query the archive.
evidence.weak: Keeps a full year in the search cluster.

misconceptions.pattern: Believes keeping all logs in one search cluster is simplest.
misconceptions.challenge: Roughly how many terabytes is a year of logs, and what does indexing all of it cost?

probes: How would an engineer search logs from months ago?
How do logs move from hot to archive?
hints: Recent logs are searched constantly, old ones rarely.
Object storage is far cheaper than a search cluster.
agenda.moveOnSummary: Hot, time-indexed search for recent logs plus a compressed, partitioned object-storage archive for a year.

agenda.goal: Keep logs flowing and searchable during incident bursts.
agenda.opener: An outage makes every service log far more errors than usual. Which part falls behind first, and what do engineers see?

evidence.strong: Identifies indexing as the bottleneck; the log broker absorbs the burst so nothing is lost and indexers fall behind; scales indexers, prioritises error and security topics, monitors and shows ingest lag so engineers know how fresh search is.
evidence.adequate: Says the broker absorbs bursts but has no plan for indexer lag or priorities.
evidence.weak: Assumes autoscaling the search cluster handles it, or accepts losing logs.

misconceptions.pattern: Thinks autoscaling the search cluster keeps up instantly.
misconceptions.challenge: Adding search nodes means moving shards between them. How quickly does that help during the incident?

probes: How do engineers know how far behind the search is?
What would you prioritise when you can't index everything at once?
hints: A durable broker lets indexing lag without losing data.
Not all topics need to catch up at the same speed.
agenda.moveOnSummary: Kafka absorbs bursts, indexers lag but nothing is lost, critical topics are prioritised and lag is visible.

agenda.goal: Decide what to shed under pressure without losing critical logs.
agenda.opener: If you truly can't keep everything during a spike, what gets dropped and what never does?

evidence.strong: Separates classes by topic: security and audit never dropped and replicated; debug sampled first; per-service quotas so one noisy service can't starve others; drops are counted and reported.
evidence.adequate: Samples everything uniformly, including security logs.
evidence.weak: Drops whatever arrives when queues are full.

misconceptions.pattern: Believes uniform random sampling is fair to all logs.
misconceptions.challenge: An attacker's login attempts are in the security log. Is sampling those acceptable?

probes: How do you stop one noisy service from crowding out everyone else?
hints: Classes of logs have different value.
Quotas per producer keep one service from dominating.
agenda.moveOnSummary: Security and audit never dropped, debug sampled first, per-service quotas, and drops reported.

agenda.goal: Turn raw lines into structured, enriched records with a path for bad ones.
agenda.opener: How do you make plain-text and JSON logs from many services searchable in the same way?

evidence.strong: A processing stage parses JSON and known text patterns into a common schema (timestamp, level, service, host, trace id, message), enriches with metadata such as pod and region, and routes unparsable lines to a dead-letter topic rather than dropping them.
evidence.adequate: Parses JSON but drops or ignores text logs.
evidence.weak: Indexes raw lines as one text blob with no structure.

misconceptions.pattern: Thinks unparsable lines can just be dropped.
misconceptions.challenge: A legacy payment service only writes plain text. What do you lose by dropping its lines?

probes: How would you search for one request across all services?
hints: A shared set of fields makes cross-service search possible.
Bad lines can be kept aside rather than lost.
agenda.moveOnSummary: Parse to a common schema, enrich with metadata and trace ids, and dead-letter unparsable lines.

agenda.goal: Keep the search index healthy as teams log arbitrary fields.
agenda.opener: A team starts logging a JSON field with a random key on every line. What happens to your index?

evidence.strong: Explains that dynamic mappings create a new field per key until the cluster's metadata explodes; enforces field limits and a logging convention, maps unknown fields into a catch-all text or flattened field, and sizes shards with time-based rollover per service.
evidence.adequate: Knows mappings can grow but has no limit or fallback.

misconceptions.pattern: Believes the search engine handles any number of fields automatically.
misconceptions.challenge: Each unique key becomes a field in the cluster's mapping. What happens after millions of unique keys?

probes: How big would you make each shard, and why does it matter?
hints: Every distinct field costs the cluster something.
Conventions and limits protect a shared index.
agenda.moveOnSummary: Field limits, logging conventions and a catch-all field prevent mapping explosion; time-based rollover keeps shards healthy.

agenda.goal: Keep secrets and personal data out of stored logs and control who reads what.
agenda.opener: How do you keep passwords, tokens and card numbers out of the logs, and who can read which logs?

evidence.strong: Redacts at the agent or the processing stage, before indexing or archiving, using pattern rules for tokens, emails and card numbers and allow-lists of fields; restricts access per team and per log class, with security logs readable only by a few, and audits searches.
evidence.adequate: Plans to redact after indexing, or has redaction but no access control.

misconceptions.pattern: Thinks redacting after the logs are stored is fine.
misconceptions.challenge: A card number reached the archive and its replicas. How do you remove it from every copy?

probes: Where in the pipeline is the earliest point you can redact?
hints: The earlier you redact, the fewer copies you have to clean.
Different teams shouldn't see every team's logs.
agenda.moveOnSummary: Redact at ingest with pattern and allow-list rules, and enforce per-team and per-class access with audit.

agenda.goal: Summarise trade-offs between search capability and cost.
agenda.opener: What are the main trade-offs in your design, especially between search power and cost?

evidence.strong: Weighs full-text indexing against label-only or columnar stores, hot retention length against cost, replicas, sampling versus completeness, and states what would change at larger scale.
evidence.weak: Says the design has no meaningful trade-offs.

misconceptions.pattern: Believes indexing everything for a year is just an infrastructure detail.
misconceptions.challenge: What dominates the monthly bill in your design?

probes: Which cost would grow fastest as the company doubles?
hints: Think about indexing cost and retention length.
Would every team need full-text search?
agenda.moveOnSummary: Search power costs money: tier aggressively, buffer bursts, and choose indexing depth per log class.

curveballs.prompt: One service ships a bug that logs the same stack trace thousands of times a second, and everyone else's logs start lagging. What do you do?
A team starts logging request headers as JSON keys, so every line brings new field names. The search cluster's heap climbs. Why, and how do you fix it?

alternatives.choice: Label-indexed log store such as Loki
alternatives.whenBetter: When logs are well structured, queries filter by service and labels, and full-text indexing cost is unjustified.

alternatives.choice: Columnar store such as ClickHouse for logs
alternatives.whenBetter: When most queries are aggregations and filters on structured fields at high volume.
When the team is small and the cost per gigabyte is acceptable.

exemplars.label: Buffered, tiered and safe
exemplars.outline: Clarifies volume, bursts, search freshness, retention and critical classes, and estimates a couple of hundred megabytes a second. Runs Fluent Bit agents with disk buffers to regional collectors and Kafka topics per class. A processing stage parses to a common schema, enriches with trace ids, redacts secrets and dead-letters bad lines. A seven-day hot tier in OpenSearch with per-service daily indices, field limits and rollover; a year archived as compressed Parquet in S3 queried with Athena. Bursts are absorbed by Kafka with security topics prioritised, debug sampled, per-service quotas and visible lag.

exemplars.label: Classic stack without guardrails
exemplars.outline: Uses agents, Kafka and Elasticsearch with an S3 archive, but samples all logs equally under pressure, allows dynamic mappings and redacts only in the search UI.

exemplars.label: Straight into the cluster
exemplars.outline: Sends logs from apps directly to one large Elasticsearch cluster kept for a year, with no buffer, no tiers, no priorities and no redaction.
